extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and academic mathematicians (authors, readers, librarians)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, consumer-side strategy for mathematicians to force lower journal prices and wider open access: do self-archiving, avoid downloading from non-free journal sites, use shaming and download-behavior to give librarians negotiating leverage, and push for structural changes in society publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of journals and editorial boards
rubrics_metrics.description: We as a community tend to like our journals more than we hate them. They compete for our papers. We know which journals are good, better or best; each journal has composed the best editorial board it could.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat existing journals and their editorial structures as important community-curated quality filters; avoid wholesale destruction of the journal nomenclature because of high replacement cost. Preserve useful editorial functions even while pushing for access reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boycott all non-free journals as a consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: Boycott all non-free journals as a consumer! Do NOT download papers from journal websites. This does not mean stop submitting, refereeing, or serving on editorial boards — those activities should continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The boycott is targeted at consumption (downloading) to deprive publishers of evidence they are indispensable. Be universal — do not pick individual publishers to boycott, but avoid all paywalled journal websites when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-archive every paper you ever wrote
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every(!) paper you ever wrote freely accessible. Not just the latest – all of them! Put them on the arXiv, viXra, your own website, or anywhere searchable by search engines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't know how, ask for help. Examples of people doing this include Noga Alon, Richard Stanley, and Paul Erdős. The author emphasizes doing it immediately ('right now') and routinely; prioritize searchability so Google Scholar can find copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer free copies via Google Scholar/author sites when reading
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading papers, don't go first to MathSciNet's automatic article button; Google Scholar usually gives multiple options including arXiv or author websites — choose those.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Google Scholar (or Microsoft Academic) to find free copies; prefer author-hosted or arXiv versions. Recommend a MathSciNet feature: add a 'web search' button next to 'article' to make it easier to avoid publisher sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anonymizing/masking techniques on campus and alternative browsers
rubrics_metrics.description: On campus, use a browser masking your IP address (e.g., Opera) or avoid remote access/VPN so that downloads from paywalled sites do not show up as campus demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the chance that library usage data will overstate dependence on publisher sites. Off-campus browsing and other standard privacy tools make it easy to avoid creating traceable download records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat freely-available journal-hosted articles (e.g., outside sliding windows) as free
rubrics_metrics.description: If a journal-hosted article is freely downloadable (for example older papers outside the 4-year sliding window used by some publishers), treat that part of the publisher as 'free' and download without notifying your library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be pragmatic: if the publisher already makes the file publicly available, download it directly without involving the library, to avoid signaling continued dependence that could weaken negotiation leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email authors and request files; shame them into posting
rubrics_metrics.description: If a desired paper isn't freely available, email the authors and request a copy, and shame them into putting the paper online if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forwarding explanatory material (such as this post) is suggested. Author requests are effective (the author reports near-100% success in practice when emailing). Use polite pressure to encourage authors to self-archive.

rubrics_metrics.name: If authors are non-responsive, repost papers online even if it violates copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper is inaccessible and the authors won't respond, download it (via library if necessary) and post it online — yes, in violation of copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author presents this as civil-disobedience-style action justified by the greater good and notes many already do this. The recommendation: after obtaining a copy, make it publicly available so others can bypass paywalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer and promote free copies on course websites
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating course websites, make all or most links point to free versions of articles; download and repost papers on course pages so students can bypass library redirects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every link to a free copy helps reduce publisher leverage. Instructors should proactively assemble free copies for students and avoid linking to paywalled publisher pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public shaming as an instrument to change behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Public shaming is one of the key instruments in the 21st century; it can shame authors or journals into posting papers, filling gaps, or retracting incorrect papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites examples where shaming worked (and where it failed). Use targeted public pressure as a tool to encourage authors and editors to make papers openly available; recognize it can be effective but is not universally successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce downloads to give librarians negotiating leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: From a librarian perspective, a rapid decrease in journal downloads (e.g., by a factor of 10 over a few years) would free librarians to cancel subscriptions and negotiate much lower prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective consumer behavior (less downloading from publisher sites) produces data librarians can use to justify non-renewal or hard bargaining. The strategy: reduce visible usage so libraries can credibly claim subscriptions are less needed and press publishers to cut prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective boycotts of specific publishers; they are counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Boycotting selective publishers gives free reign to others and often fails because people avoid boycotts that impose significant cost; selective boycotts don't produce systemic change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of targeting individual publishers, conduct a universal consumer boycott of all non-free journals. Continue academic labor (submissions, refereeing) while changing purchasing/consumption behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push for structural reforms in society publishers (e.g., AMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional societies with large publishing businesses (e.g., AMS) have conflicts of interest; ideally they should sell their journal business to a university press or create a 'Chinese wall' separating publishing from political activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rationale: societies dependent on publishing revenue are less likely to advocate for open access. Structural separation or divestment would allow reinvestment in free publishing initiatives and reduce conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternative search engines and overseas depositaries for hard-to-find papers
rubrics_metrics.description: If Google Scholar fails, consider other search engines (Yandex, DuckDuckGo) or overseas depositaries which may be less strict about copyright and can yield download locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools can sometimes find copies not surfaced by mainstream engines. Use responsibly according to your risk tolerance; the author notes occasional reliance on overseas depositaries for convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept arXiv-overlay / scaled-down journal production as a likely future
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological and cultural changes will likely turn many journals into arXiv-overlay style publications with substantially scaled-down technical production and lower cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame reform efforts toward enabling overlay models and accepting a future where publishers provide reduced technical services and print only for archival or symbolic reasons; reallocate savings to research personnel and student support.
